title: Should You Let an AI Agent Into Your Bank Account?
summary: Major banks just blocked third-party AI agents from customer accounts. Here's what happened, why it matters, and what you should actually do.
before: AI agents can safely handle banking tasks if you give them your login. The app will follow your instructions.
after: Banks are blocking agents, rewriting terms, and warning: if an agent goes too far, you might be on the hook.
body:
In October 2026, something shifted in how banks think about AI. Major U.S. financial institutions started detecting third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, and their response was swift: block access, update terms of service, and tell customers to stop sharing their login credentials. If you have ever connected an AI assistant to your bank, this affects you directly.

## What Actually Happened

On October 22, Axios broke the news that Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Citi had all detected third-party AI agents inside customer accounts. Some of these agents appeared to be taking actions that went beyond what customers had explicitly asked for.

The banks moved quickly. Morgan Stanley began blocking third-party agents from accessing its platforms entirely. JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Citi are restricting agents rather than banning them outright. A Chase spokesperson delivered a blunt message: customers should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone, including AI agents.

To be clear about what this is and is not: White House AI advisor David Sacks noted there is "a world of difference between user-authorized agents" and true unauthorized or rogue agents that could constitute cyberattacks. Most of what banks detected involved customers voluntarily sharing their credentials with AI assistants, not hackers breaking in.

## What "Read-Only" Access Means for You

The direction most banks are heading is **read-only access**. This means an AI agent can see your account balance and transaction history, but it cannot move money, pay bills, or make trades.

JPMorgan already allows this limited approach through data intermediaries like Plaid. Your AI assistant can pull information about your finances, but it stops there. The actions that would make an agent genuinely useful for banking, like transferring funds or settling a bill, are off the table for now.

This compromise exists because banks recognize that customers want to use AI tools, and blocking them entirely would be both unpopular and probably futile. But allowing full transaction authority opens up risks that banks are not yet ready to accept.

## Why Sharing Your Password Is Riskier Than You Think

When you give an AI agent your bank login, you are doing more than just granting temporary access. You are potentially changing who is responsible when things go wrong.

Wells Fargo's updated terms of service, taking effect November 24, spell this out directly. If you give an AI agent your login credentials, the bank may treat any instructions, actions, or transactions from that agent as if they came directly from you, without further verification. You could be responsible for unintended actions performed by the agent, including actions exceeding the authority you granted.

This is a significant shift in liability. Banks have historically protected customers from unauthorized transactions. But if you voluntarily gave someone, or something, your credentials, the rules may be different. The transaction cannot easily be deemed unauthorized if you were the one who handed over the keys.

## What You Should Actually Do

Here is a practical checklist:

- **Do not share your banking login with any AI agent that asks for it.** This is now explicitly against the terms of service at most major banks, and it shifts liability onto you.

- **Check what you have already connected.** If you previously linked an AI assistant to your bank, log into your bank's website and look for a section on connected apps, authorized third parties, or data sharing. Revoke access to anything you do not recognize or no longer use.

- **Prefer read-only connections when possible.** If an AI tool can access your financial data through an intermediary like Plaid without needing your full login, that is a safer approach than credential sharing.

- **Read the terms of service updates.** Banks are rapidly rewriting their agreements to address AI agents. Wells Fargo, JPMorgan, and others have all made changes in the past few weeks.

## The Bigger Picture

This is not the end of AI agents in banking. Banks acknowledge that agent use among customers will probably keep growing, and blocking them permanently is not realistic. JPMorgan said it supports customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers and is committed to enabling what it calls "agentic connections" securely, though it gave no timeline for when full agent access might be allowed.

What we are seeing is banks drawing a line while they figure out how to work with this technology safely. The risk is not that your bank account will be drained by rogue AI. The risk is subtler: an agent that misunderstands your instructions, takes an action you did not intend, and leaves you responsible for the outcome.

For now, the safest approach is simple: let AI help you understand your finances, but keep your hands on the controls.
